Manshu LLM: A Character-Level Transformer Language Model Built from Scratch# #LLM; #Transformer; #PyTorch; #FastAPI
Every LLM component (embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding window, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head) implemented from scratch, with both local and HTTP inference services.
Repository: (not public yet; local project manshu_llm)
The flowchart below summarizes the main pipeline, “data preparation → training → inference/serving”, along with the data flow of the model’s forward pass.
graph TD A[Tiny Shakespeare] --> B[download_data] B --> C[tokenize_data] C --> D[train.npy val.npy vocab] D --> E[train.py] E --> F[checkpoints] F --> G[infer.py] F --> H[serve.py] H --> I["/generate"] H --> J["/health"] K[Input IDs] --> L[Token Embedding] L --> M[Transformer Block x N] M --> N[RMSNorm LM Head] N --> O[Logits] Project Overview# Manshu LLM (v0.1.0) is one of my flagship projects, with two core emphases: implementing every LLM component from scratch (embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head, etc.) and providing a complete inference service (local scripts plus a FastAPI HTTP API with greedy/sampling decoding and health checks). The project covers the full pipeline of “data preparation → training → checkpoint management → inference service”, demonstrating a deep understanding of Transformers and LLM engineering. It uses character-level modeling, so no BPE or WordPiece is needed and the vocabulary is derived from the data. The default dataset is Tiny Shakespeare, which suits small-scale experiments and teaching.
Tech stack: a decoder-only Transformer in PyTorch featuring GQA (grouped-query attention), RoPE (rotary position embeddings), sliding-window attention, a SwiGLU FFN, and Pre-RMSNorm, aligned with mainstream architectures such as Llama. Training uses AdamW, cosine/linear learning-rate scheduling, and gradient accumulation, all configured through YAML (configs/model.yaml, train.yaml, data.yaml). Inference supports greedy decoding and temperature / top-k / top-p sampling. The service is built with FastAPI + Uvicorn, exposing POST /generate (text generation) and GET /health (health check), with API docs at /docs and /redoc. Docker deployment is supported (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, and build.sh under docker/). Project layout: llm/ (model, data, training, inference, utils), scripts/ (download_data, tokenize_data, train, infer, check_model), configs/, data/ (raw, processed, vocab), checkpoints/, and serve.py at the root.
Highlights# Every LLM component built from scratch: no reliance on Hugging Face or other model libraries. Token embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and the LM head are all hand-written, which builds a solid grasp of the math and implementation details while staying aligned with architectures like Llama. Complete inference service: local inference (infer.py, greedy/temperature/top-k/top-p sampling) and an HTTP inference service (FastAPI POST /generate, GET /health, Pydantic request/response models, CORS, Docker deployment) that can serve text generation directly. End-to-end pipeline: data preparation → training → checkpoint management → inference service; a single project demonstrates the full engineering path “from raw corpus to a callable text-generation service”. Reproducible and configurable: YAML separates model/training/data configs, and training and inference share the same keys and loading logic, making experiments easy to reproduce and hyperparameters easy to switch. Character-level simplicity: a small vocabulary and simple implementation allow fast validation of architecture and hyperparameters on small corpora like Tiny Shakespeare, ideal for teaching and for walking through in interviews. My Role and Contributions# I handled full-stack development of the model, training, inference, and serving, with a focus on:
Implementing the LLM components: built the decoder-only Transformer’s token embedding, GroupedQueryAttention, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and LM head from scratch, including weight initialization and options like tie_word_embeddings; every submodule is hand-written with no model-library dependencies. Providing the inference service: implemented local inference (infer.py + greedy_decode / sample_decode with temperature, top_k, top_p) and an HTTP inference service (FastAPI POST /generate, GET /health, Pydantic request/response models, model loading in lifespan, CORS, Docker deployment) offering text generation and health checks out of the box. Data and training: CharTokenizer, CharDataset, collate_fn; a Trainer (gradient accumulation, checkpoint management, validation), AdamW, learning-rate scheduling, and loss/optimizer wrappers. Category Technology Purpose Deep learning framework PyTorch Model implementation, training, and inference Model architecture Decoder-only Transformer Backbone of the character-level LM Attention GQA + RoPE + sliding window Grouped queries, positional encoding, long-context optimization FFN / normalization SwiGLU + RMSNorm Feed-forward network and Pre-Norm Training AdamW + Cosine/Linear LR + gradient accumulation Optimizer and learning-rate scheduling Configuration YAML (configs/) Model, training, and data configs API service FastAPI + Uvicorn Text generation and health checks Deployment Docker (optional) Containerized runtime Background# Implementing a language model from scratch builds a deep understanding of every part of a Transformer: embeddings, attention, positional encoding, FFN, loss, and sampling. Simply calling existing libraries makes it hard to master the details of GQA, RoPE, and sliding windows, or their impact on memory and long sequences. This project implements every LLM component from scratch and ties “model architecture → data pipeline → training loop → inference service (local + HTTP API)” into a single runnable, configurable codebase, making it easy to experiment with different layer counts, window sizes, and sampling strategies. It serves as a flagship project demonstrating deep understanding of Transformers and LLM engineering, highlighting the full-stack ability to “implement every component and ship an inference service” on a resume or portfolio.
Why character-level? Character-level modeling needs no BPE/WordPiece; the vocabulary is derived from the data and is small, so implementation and debugging are simple, and architecture and hyperparameters can be validated quickly on small corpora like Tiny Shakespeare. To move to subword tokenization later, only the tokenizer and vocabulary path need to change; the existing training and inference pipelines can be reused.
Choosing character-level over subword/word-level prioritizes interpretability and fast experiment iteration in this project. For larger corpora and stronger results, subword tokenization and larger configurations can be plugged into the same codebase.
System Architecture and Design Choices# The overall design is single-machine training with a single-process service.
Data flow: raw text (e.g., data/raw/tiny_shakespeare.txt) is read by tokenize_data.py → CharTokenizer.build_vocab(text) counts characters to build the vocabulary (<unk>=0 + characters sorted by frequency) → tokenizer.encode(text) produces a 1D array of token IDs → split into training/validation segments by val_ratio → saved as train.npy, val.npy (dtype int32), and char_vocab.json.
Training flow: CharDataset(data_path, tokenizer, context_window) slides a window over the 1D array; each sample is a contiguous slice of length context_window+1, with the first context_window tokens as input_ids and the last context_window as target_ids (targets are the inputs shifted right by one). collate_fn stacks equal-length samples into (batch_size, seq_len), padding with pad_token_id=0 if lengths differ. Before each batch enters the model, a causal mask (L, L) is built from seq_len; the forward pass yields logits (B, L, vocab_size), and the loss is CrossEntropyLoss(logits, target_ids) (with ignore_index=-1 support). Within the accumulation window only backward runs; once gradient_accumulation_steps is reached, gradient clipping, optimizer.step, and scheduler.step are executed. Every eval_steps the model is evaluated on the validation set and a best checkpoint is saved if validation loss improves; every save_steps a periodic checkpoint is saved, capped by save_total_limit.
Inference/serving flow: on startup, infer.py or serve reads the three YAML files via load_all_configs(config_dir), takes vocab_dir from the data config to locate char_vocab.json, and loads the CharTokenizer. It builds the Transformer from the model config (injecting vocab_size=tokenizer.vocab_size), then loads weights with load_model_only(model, checkpoint_path). At inference time the prompt is encoded (an empty prompt starts from [[0]], i.e., <unk>), greedy_decode or sample_decode is chosen based on temperature, and the output is decoded to text. The server performs this loading inside FastAPI’s lifespan, and incoming requests call the generation logic directly; results are currently returned all at once (non-streaming).
Design rationale: PyTorch makes it easy to implement each module from scratch and to do gradient checks and shape debugging. GQA reduces the number of KV heads, enabling longer sequences or larger batches at the same parameter count. RoPE encodes position into Q/K, removing the need for an explicit positional embedding table. Sliding windows limit the attention span, lowering memory and compute for long sequences. SwiGLU and RMSNorm are standard in modern LLMs and help convergence and numerical stability. FastAPI and Pydantic make it easy to define request/response models and auto-generate OpenAPI docs, simplifying integration and frontend hookup.
Architecture alignment: the attention and FFN design in this project (GQA, RoPE, sliding window, SwiGLU, RMSNorm) matches open-source LLMs such as Llama and Mistral, so the understanding gained here transfers to tuning and extending larger models and existing libraries (e.g., Hugging Face).
Key Design Rationale# GQA (grouped-query attention)
Multiple query heads share one set of key/value heads, preserving expressiveness while reducing the KV cache and compute. This allows larger batches or sequence lengths under limited memory and matches current open-source LLM practice. Configured via num_attention_heads and num_key_value_heads (num_heads must be divisible by num_kv_heads).
RoPE (rotary position embeddings)
Position is encoded as rotations of Q and K, so relative position is represented by angles. This supports extrapolation and longer contexts, needs no positional embedding table in the embedding layer, and is compatible with GQA and sliding windows. Configured via max_position_embeddings and rope_theta (default 10000.0); RoPE is built per head_dim inside each block and passed into the attention layer.
Sliding-window attention
Each position attends only to tokens within a local window, reducing attention complexity from quadratic in sequence length to a function of window size, which significantly cuts memory and compute for long-sequence training and inference. Implementation: compute QK^T to get scores, then call apply_sliding_window_mask. With sliding_window_overlap=True the window is symmetric (position i attends to [max(0, i-w/2), min(L, i+w/2+1)]); with False it is an asymmetric causal window ([max(0, i-w+1), i+1]). The window mask is ANDed with the causal lower-triangular mask, invisible positions in scores are set to -inf, then softmax is applied and multiplied by V.
SwiGLU + RMSNorm
SwiGLU strengthens the FFN via element-wise multiplication of a gate and an up-projection (gate_proj → SiLU, up_proj → element-wise multiply → down_proj). RMSNorm replaces LayerNorm to reduce compute and dependencies, and the Pre-Norm structure (norm before each sublayer, then residual) improves stability in deep networks, consistent with Llama and similar architectures.
YAML configs + unified loading
Model, training, and data parameters are separated into configs/model.yaml, train.yaml, and data.yaml, and loaded into a single dict (keys “model”, “train”, “data”) via load_all_configs(config_dir). Training, inference, and serving share the same paths and keys, making it easy to reproduce experiments and switch device, step counts, window size, and other hyperparameters.
Features# Health Checks# The service exposes GET /health for liveness probes and load balancing:
Response body (Pydantic model HealthResponse): status (healthy / model_not_loaded), model_loaded (boolean), device (e.g., cuda:0 or cpu), model_info (optional; includes num_layers, hidden_size, total_params, vocab_size) Startup: lifespan loads the config, tokenizer, model, and checkpoint in order; if any step fails an exception is raised and the service does not start Errors: if the model is not loaded at runtime, POST /generate returns 503 with detail “model not loaded” Data Preparation# download_data.py: downloads the Tiny Shakespeare raw text from Karpathy’s char-rnn repository, saves it to data/raw/tiny_shakespeare.txt, and prints the character count (URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/char-rnn/master/data/tinyshakespeare/input.txt). tokenize_data.py: reads val_ratio (default 0.1) from configs/data.yaml; reads the raw text; instantiates CharTokenizer() and calls build_vocab(text) (counts characters with Counter, <unk>=0, the rest sorted by frequency); saves the vocabulary to data/vocab/char_vocab.json; encode(text) produces the full list of token IDs; splits it proportionally into training/validation segments, converts them to int32 numpy arrays, and saves them as data/processed/train.npy and data/processed/val.npy. Input/output paths are hard-coded in the script, matching the “download first, then tokenize” workflow. CharTokenizer (llm/data/tokenizer.py): char_to_id, id_to_char, vocab_size; build_vocab(texts) builds the vocabulary from text; encode(text) looks up each character to produce an ID list, mapping unknown characters to <unk> (id 0); decode(ids) converts an ID list back to a string; save_vocab/load_vocab read and write JSON. The vocabulary JSON is a character-to-id mapping.
Outputs: train.npy, val.npy (1D int32 arrays) and char_vocab.json (character → id). Data statistics (character count, token count, train/validation split, vocabulary size) are printed at the end of tokenize_data.
Model Architecture# llm/model/transformer.py: the main model. Input input_ids (batch_size, seq_len) passes through TokenEmbedding to get (B, L, hidden_size), then N TransformerBlocks, a final RMSNorm, and finally the LM head (or the transposed shared embedding) to produce logits (B, L, vocab_size). Supports tie_word_embeddings: when True there is no separate lm_head and the output is F.linear(x, embedding.weight). llm/model/block.py: a single TransformerBlock. First attn_norm(x) → GQA (with RoPE, sliding_window, mask) → residual; then ffn_norm(x) → FFN (SwiGLU) → residual. Input and output shapes are both (B, L, hidden_size). llm/model/attention.py: GroupedQueryAttention (independent Q heads; shared K/V heads repeated to match the number of Q heads) and MultiHeadAttention. scaled_dot_product_attention computes scores, applies the sliding-window mask (if configured), then the causal/general mask, and multiplies the softmax by V. create_causal_mask(seq_len) returns a lower-triangular boolean mask; apply_sliding_window_mask(scores, window_size, seq_len, overlap) combines the window mask with the causal mask and writes it into scores. llm/model/ffn.py: SwiGLU: gate_proj(x) → SiLU, up_proj(x) → element-wise multiply → down_proj; output keeps the input hidden_size. llm/model/rope.py: RoPE built from head_dim, max_seq_len, and theta, applying rotary position encoding to Q and K. llm/model/norm.py: RMSNorm(dim, eps); forward computes x / sqrt(mean(x^2)+eps) * weight. llm/model/embedding.py: token embedding, vocab_size → hidden_size. Core features: Pre-Norm (RMSNorm before each sublayer), GQA, RoPE, sliding window (symmetric/asymmetric), SwiGLU, RMSNorm, and optional tying of word embeddings and LM head (tie_word_embeddings). Weight initialization can be enabled via llm.utils.init.apply_llm_init (init_weights and init_std in model.yaml).
Training Pipeline# scripts/train.py: loads the configs (model, train, data), builds CharDataset(train_path, tokenizer, context_window) and CharDataset(val_path, …), with DataLoaders using collate_fn (from llm.data.collate); instantiates the Transformer (with vocab_size injected into the config) and the Trainer; runs Trainer.train(). llm/training/trainer.py: train_step(batch): batch is (input_ids, target_ids), both shaped (batch_size, seq_len); creates a causal mask (seq_len, seq_len); logits = model(input_ids, mask=causal_mask); loss = criterion(logits, target_ids), divided by gradient_accumulation_steps before backward; when (global_step+1) % gradient_accumulation_steps == 0, runs gradient clipping (max_grad_norm, default 1.0), optimizer.step, zero_grad, and scheduler.step; global_step increments by 1 each step. evaluate(max_batches): runs a no-grad forward pass over val_loader and averages the loss. save_checkpoint(is_best): writes the file via utils.checkpoint.save_checkpoint; when is_best, names it best_model_step_.pt and deletes the old best; otherwise names it checkpoint_step_.pt and maintains a saved_checkpoints queue, deleting the oldest file when save_total_limit is exceeded. Training loop: iterates over num_epochs, running train_step per batch; every eval_steps runs evaluate and calls save_checkpoint(is_best=True) if validation loss beats best_val_loss; every save_steps, if no best was saved at that step, calls save_checkpoint(is_best=False); supports early termination via max_steps. llm/training/optim.py: AdamW (learning_rate, weight_decay, beta1, beta2, eps); learning-rate scheduler options cosine, linear, and constant, with warmup_steps. llm/training/loss.py: CrossEntropyLoss(logits, targets) flattens logits and targets and calls F.cross_entropy, with ignore_index support (default -1). CharDataset: __len__ = len(data) - context_window; __getitem__(idx) takes data[idx:idx+context_window+1], with the first context_window tokens as input_ids and the last context_window as target_ids (targets are inputs shifted right by one), returning two 1D LongTensors.
Checkpoints: best_model_step_.pt (best validation loss; only the latest is kept) and checkpoint_step_.pt (periodic; count limited by save_total_limit), both saved in checkpoint_dir from train.yaml (default checkpoints).
Inference and Sampling# llm/inference/generate.py: greedy_decode(model, input_ids, max_length, device, stop_token_ids): at each step, runs a forward pass on the current generated_ids, takes the argmax of logits[:, -1, :] as the next token, and appends it to the sequence; supports a stop_token_ids list, marking a sequence finished when hit and exiting early once all are finished. sample_decode(model, input_ids, max_length, temperature, top_k, top_p, device, stop_token_ids): with temperature=0 it calls greedy_decode directly; otherwise each step divides logits[:, -1, :] by temperature, optionally applies top_k (keep the k largest logits) and top_p (nucleus: sort by probability and cut positions whose cumulative probability exceeds p), then applies softmax and samples with multinomial; also supports stop_token_ids. The current implementation runs a forward pass over the whole sequence at each step and does not use a KV cache. scripts/infer.py: checkpoint, prompt, max_length, temperature, top_k, top_p, config_dir, device_str, and num_samples are configurable at the top of the script. It loads the config and vocabulary (vocab_dir from data_config, path vocab_dir/char_vocab.json), creates the model, and loads weights with load_model_only. A non-empty prompt is encoded and reshaped to (1, seq_len); an empty prompt uses input_ids = [[0]] ( as the start token). Greedy or sampling decoding is chosen by temperature; if num_samples>1, multiple samples are generated in a loop. After decoding, if there is a prompt and the generated text starts with it, the “full” and “new” parts are printed separately; otherwise the full text is printed, along with character and token counts. Sampling strategy: temperature=0 means greedy; temperature>0 means sampling, combined with top_k (0 disables) and top_p (0.0 disables) to balance diversity and coherence.
Text Generation API# serve.py: a FastAPI app whose lifespan loads the configs, CharTokenizer(vocab_path), Transformer(model_config), and load_model_only(model, checkpoint_path), storing the model and tokenizer as globals. CONFIG sets checkpoint_path, config_dir, vocab_path, device (cuda if available, else cpu), host (0.0.0.0), and port (8000). POST /generate: the request body is GenerateRequest (Pydantic): prompt (required, e.g. “First Citizen:\n”), max_length (default 100, ge=1, le=1000), temperature (default 0.8, ge=0, le=2), top_k (default 50, ge=0, le=200), top_p (default 0.9, ge=0, le=1), num_samples (default 1, ge=1, le=5). The response body is GenerateResponse: prompt, samples (a list, each with text and tokens), and model_info (checkpoint, device, total_params, num_layers, hidden_size). temperature=0 calls greedy_decode, otherwise sample_decode; the output is decoded with tokenizer.decode, packed into a list of GeneratedSample, and returned. CORS is configured (allow_origins=["*"]) for cross-origin frontend access. Results are currently returned all at once, not streamed. GET / returns a welcome message and the endpoint list (generate, health, docs, redoc). If the model is not loaded, /generate returns 503 with detail “model not loaded”; errors during generation return 500 with detail “generation failed: …”. Running and Deployment# Typical workflow: run download_data.py to download Tiny Shakespeare, then tokenize_data.py to produce train.npy, val.npy, and char_vocab.json; then run scripts/train.py to train, with checkpoints written to checkpoint_dir (default checkpoints/). After training, use scripts/infer.py for local inference, or start serve.py to expose POST /generate and GET /health. For Docker deployment, see the docker/ directory (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, build.sh).
Quick start: after training, run python serve.py and open http://localhost:8000/docs to try POST /generate (text generation) and GET /health (health check) interactively; the root path GET / returns a welcome message and the endpoint list.
Helper Scripts and Configuration# scripts/check_model.py: inspects model structure or weights (e.g., parameter count, shapes) for debugging and alignment. configs/model.yaml: num_hidden_layers, hidden_size, num_attention_heads, num_key_value_heads, intermediate_size, max_position_embeddings, rope_theta, sliding_window, sliding_window_overlap, rms_norm_eps, tie_word_embeddings, init_weights, init_std, etc. configs/train.yaml: learning_rate, weight_decay, beta1, beta2, eps, lr_scheduler (cosine/linear/constant), warmup_steps, max_steps, batch_size, gradient_accumulation_steps, max_grad_norm, save_steps, eval_steps, save_total_limit, device, num_epochs, checkpoint_dir, use_amp, amp_dtype, etc. configs/data.yaml: processed_dir, vocab_dir, context_window, num_workers, pin_memory, val_ratio, etc. Technical Challenges and Solutions# During implementation, targeted designs addressed masking and causality, training stability and long sequences, and a unified entry point for inference and serving, enabling stable training on limited resources and a consistent external service interface.
Sliding-Window Attention and Causal Masking# Challenge: the mask must guarantee causality (each token sees only the past) while restricting attention to a local window, so it has to satisfy both the lower-triangular and window-boundary constraints and fit the Q/K/V shapes of RoPE and GQA. If window and causal masks are applied separately, ordering and broadcasting must be consistent to avoid missing or duplicate masking.
Solution: in scaled_dot_product_attention, first compute QK^T / sqrt(head_dim) to get scores (B, H, L, L). If sliding_window is configured, call apply_sliding_window_mask(scores, window_size, seq_len, overlap), which builds window_mask (symmetric window [i-w/2, i+w/2+1] when overlap=True, asymmetric [i-w+1, i+1] when False), ANDs it with the causal lower-triangular mask, and sets invisible positions in scores to -inf. If an external mask (e.g., a causal mask) is also passed, scores are masked_fill’ed according to its boolean values (False becomes -inf). This applies the window first, then causality, and an (L, L) mask is unsqueezed to (1, 1, L, L) to match the scores dimensions. Each block passes sliding_window and sliding_window_overlap from the config, and the attention layer uniformly uses GQA + RoPE + this masking logic.
Training Stability and Long Sequences# Challenge: deep Transformers and longer context_window values can cause unstable gradients or out-of-memory errors; large batches are infeasible on a single GPU, and the loss curve needs to be smooth.
Solution: Pre-RMSNorm plus gradient clipping (max_grad_norm, default 1.0), running clip_grad_norm_ before each optimizer.step. AdamW (with weight_decay) and a cosine learning-rate schedule with warmup_steps avoid an overly high early learning rate. gradient_accumulation_steps accumulates gradients over smaller per-step batches before updating, emulating a larger batch while keeping per-step memory under control. Sliding windows limit the attention span, allowing a larger context_window or batch_size within the same memory. The config optionally enables use_amp and amp_dtype (e.g., bfloat16) to further save memory and speed things up. The loss can use ignore_index (e.g., -1) for padding positions; in the current dataset equal-length samples are stacked directly by collate, so with no padding nothing needs to be ignored. If variable lengths are supported in the future, pad positions in target_ids can be filled with -1.
Unified Entry Point for Inference and Serving# Challenge: both infer.py and serve.py must load the same model and tokenizer, consistent with the config and vocabulary path used in training, to avoid scattered configs causing load failures or dimension mismatches (e.g., vocab_size or hidden_size inconsistent with the checkpoint).
Solution: both read the three YAML files via load_all_configs(config_dir), yielding model, train, and data sub-dicts. For the vocabulary path, infer takes vocab_dir from data_config and joins vocab_dir / "char_vocab.json", while serve’s CONFIG hard-codes vocab_path (e.g., data/vocab/char_vocab.json). Before constructing the model, model_config[“vocab_size”] is set to tokenizer.vocab_size and passed into Transformer(config), keeping it consistent with training (the training script likewise injects vocab_size from the tokenizer). The checkpoint path is configured separately in serve’s CONFIG and in the variables at the top of infer, and must match the training output filename (e.g., best_model.pt or best_model_step_*.pt). Training, inference, and serving thus share the same config keys and loading logic, differing only in the entry point (script variables vs. CONFIG).
Summary# As a flagship personal project, Manshu LLM highlights two things: first, implementing every LLM component from scratch (token embedding, GQA, RoPE, sliding-window attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, LM head, etc.) without relying on model libraries; second, providing a complete inference service (local infer.py plus FastAPI POST /generate and GET /health) with greedy/sampling decoding and health checks, ready to serve text generation. The project covers the full pipeline from data preparation, training, and checkpoint management to the inference service, with YAML configuration and Docker deployment options.
Future directions: add a KV cache to inference and the API to speed up long-sequence generation; support streaming responses (e.g., SSE); wrap the model and tokenizer in Hugging Face-style from_pretrained/save_pretrained; and add more datasets and evaluation metrics to compare architectures and hyperparameters.

Manshu RAG Knowledge Base and Chat Backend# #RAG; #FastAPI
Repository: Manshu RAG Knowledge Base and Chat Backend
The flowchart below summarizes the two main paths: “document upload and parsing” and “user question and streaming answer”.
graph TD A[User uploads document] --> B[Chunked upload to MinIO] B --> C[Track chunk progress in Redis] C --> D{All chunks done?} D -->|No| B D -->|Yes| E[Merge file] E --> F[Write metadata to MySQL] F --> G[Publish Kafka message] G --> H[Kafka consumer] H --> I[Parse document with Tika] I --> J[Split text into chunks] J --> K[Call OpenAI Embedding] K --> L[Write to Elasticsearch] L --> M[Write to DocumentVector table] N[User asks a question] --> O[Embed the question] O --> P[Elasticsearch hybrid search] P --> Q[Get Top-K results] Q --> R[Assemble prompt] R --> S[OpenAI streaming generation] S --> T[Push via WebSocket] Project Overview# The Manshu backend covers the full pipeline of “upload documents → parse and index → semantic/keyword retrieval → chat with an LLM grounded in the retrieved results”. I was responsible for the AI and backend development on this project.
Tech stack: Python + FastAPI as the main framework, MySQL for business data and metadata, Redis for sessions, rate limiting and CAPTCHAs, MinIO for files and raw documents, Elasticsearch for hybrid vector and full-text search, and Kafka to split parsing and embedding into async jobs. Both chat and embeddings use OpenAI (embedding defaults to text-embedding-3-small, chat defaults to gpt-3.5-turbo; both are configurable). Deployment uses Docker + Uvicorn. All APIs share the /api/v1 prefix; chat runs over WebSocket at /api/v1/chat, with the JWT passed via the token query parameter.
Category Technology Purpose Backend framework Python + FastAPI REST API and WebSocket service Database MySQL Business data and metadata storage Cache Redis Session management, rate limiting, CAPTCHAs Object storage MinIO File and raw document storage Search engine Elasticsearch Hybrid vector and full-text search Message queue Kafka Async document parsing and embedding jobs LLM OpenAI Embedding (text-embedding-3-small) and Chat (gpt-3.5-turbo) Document parsing Apache Tika Multi-format document parsing Deployment Docker + Uvicorn Containerized deployment and ASGI server Background# As the volume of internal documents grew, plain keyword search could no longer meet the need for “semantic retrieval + LLM-generated answers grounded in retrieved results”. Documents also come in many formats (PDF, Word, Excel, PPT, HTML, Markdown, etc.), requiring a unified parsing and ingestion flow. This project chains upload, parsing, retrieval and chat into a configurable, observable pipeline, with multi-tenant isolation based on permissions and organization tags. Health checks and structured logging make operations and troubleshooting easier.
Health checks expose /health (fast liveness probe) and /health/detailed (deep probe); the latter verifies connectivity and connection pool status for MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch, MinIO and Kafka. On startup the app connects to these components in dependency order. If the Kafka consumer fails to start, only a warning is logged and the app keeps serving requests; only document parsing and embedding are temporarily unavailable.
Architecture and Technology Choices# The system uses a decoupled frontend/backend architecture: the frontend talks to the backend over HTTP and WebSocket, and the backend provides REST APIs and a WebSocket chat endpoint. Requests first pass JWT verification and Redis rate limiting before reaching business logic. Uploaded files are stored in MinIO, metadata is written to MySQL, and a parsing job is published to the Kafka document_parse topic. On the consumer side, Apache Tika parses the document, the text is split into chunks (chunk size 500, overlap 50), OpenAI Embedding is called, and vectors and metadata are written to Elasticsearch and MySQL respectively. When a user asks a question, the question is embedded first, then Elasticsearch runs vector search (dense_vector, 1536 dimensions, cosine similarity) and IK full-text search (ik_max_word for indexing, ik_smart for querying) in parallel. The two result sets are score-normalized and fused with configurable weights (default: vector 0.7, full-text 0.3). The Top-K chunks are inserted into the prompt, OpenAI generates a streaming response, and it is pushed to the frontend over the same WebSocket.
Rationale: Elasticsearch supports both vector and full-text search in the same index, so dense_vector plus IK tokenization is enough to implement hybrid search with tunable weights. Parsing and embedding are slow, so processing them asynchronously through Kafka avoids blocking the upload API and makes it easy to add more consumers and retry policies later. Tika covers common formats such as PDF, Office, HTML and Markdown, and falls back to UTF-8 decoding for plain text when parsing fails. FastAPI has solid async and WebSocket support and auto-generates OpenAPI docs, which simplifies frontend integration and API contract management.
Key Technology Rationale# Elasticsearch
Supports both semantic (vector) and keyword (full-text) retrieval in the same index. dense_vector combined with IK tokenization enables hybrid search with adjustable weights, making it easy to balance “semantic similarity” against “keyword matches”.
Kafka
Parsing and embedding take a long time; running them synchronously would easily cause upload timeouts. Async processing through Kafka lets uploads respond quickly and makes it easy to add more consumers, retries and dead-letter handling later.
Apache Tika
Covers common formats such as PDF, Office, HTML and Markdown. When parsing fails, it falls back to UTF-8 decoding for plain text, reducing the impact of a single failed file on the overall pipeline.
Features# Health Checks# The system provides two levels of health checks for load balancer integration and monitoring/alerting:
Basic check: /health, a fast liveness probe used by load balancer health checks Detailed check: /health/detailed, a deep probe that verifies connectivity and connection pool status for MySQL, Redis, Elasticsearch, MinIO and Kafka On startup the app connects to these components in dependency order. If the Kafka consumer fails to start, only a warning is logged and the app continues to serve everything except document parsing.
Authentication and Authorization# Provides registration, login, image CAPTCHAs and email verification codes, plus JWT issuance and verification. Expiration and length of CAPTCHAs and email codes are configurable. Redis-based per-endpoint rate limiting gives image CAPTCHA, email code and registration endpoints their own windows and limits (e.g. CAPTCHA requests per IP per minute) to prevent brute-force attempts and abuse. A JWT is returned on successful login and sent on subsequent requests via the Authorization header or the token query parameter.
Core features:
Image CAPTCHA generation and verification (stored in Redis, configurable expiration) Email verification code delivery (SMTP config, configurable length and expiration) JWT issuance and verification (via Authorization header or query parameter) Redis-based per-endpoint rate limiting (separate windows for image CAPTCHA, email code and registration endpoints) Rate limiting policy:
Limit on CAPTCHA requests per IP per minute Limit on email code requests per IP per minute Limit on registration requests per IP per minute File and Document Management# Uploads support chunking: each chunk is first uploaded to a temporary MinIO directory, with chunk progress tracked in Redis. Once all chunks are done, the merge API produces the final file and writes it to MySQL (file metadata, user, organization tag, public flag), then publishes a parsing job to the Kafka topic document_parse. The consumer fetches the file from MinIO, parses it with Tika, chunks it, calls Embedding per chunk, and writes vectors to Elasticsearch and metadata to the DocumentVector table. Supported formats depend on Tika and include PDF, Word, Excel, PPT, HTML, Markdown, TXT, RTF and more. On parse failure the error is logged; if needed, only metadata is persisted and the same message is not consumed again, so a single failure cannot block the queue. Document listing, deletion and related APIs are tied to permissions and organization tags, so users can only operate on data they are authorized to access.
Chunked upload: each chunk is first uploaded to a temporary MinIO directory, with progress tracked in Redis File merge: once all chunks are done, the merge API produces the final file and writes it to MySQL Job dispatch: a parsing job is published to the Kafka topic document_parse Async processing: the consumer fetches the file from MinIO, parses it with Tika, chunks it, calls Embedding per chunk and writes to Elasticsearch Supported formats: PDF, Word, Excel, PPT, HTML, Markdown, TXT, RTF and more (via Tika)
Fault tolerance: On parse failure the error is logged; if needed, only metadata is persisted and the same message is not consumed again, avoiding queue blockage.
Hybrid Search# The query text is embedded with the same Embedding model, then Elasticsearch runs vector search and IK full-text search in parallel. The two scores are normalized and merged with configurable weights, and results are isolated by user_id, org_tag and is_public so only chunks the current user may access are returned. Index fields include file_md5, chunk_id, text_content, vector, user_id, org_tag, is_public, file_name and model_version, supporting access control and result traceability.
Retrieval flow:
Embed the question (text-embedding-3-small, 1536 dimensions) Run two queries in parallel: Vector search: dense_vector field, cosine similarity Full-text search: IK tokenization (ik_max_word for indexing, ik_smart for querying) Normalize scores and merge with configurable weights (default: vector 0.7, full-text 0.3) Isolate data by user_id, org_tag and is_public Index fields: file_md5, chunk_id, text_content, vector, user_id, org_tag, is_public, file_name, model_version
Streaming Chat# The WebSocket path is /api/v1/chat. On connect, the client passes token (JWT) in the query string and optionally conversation_id (a new conversation is created if omitted). The flow is: receive user message → hybrid search for context → assemble prompt → call OpenAI streaming generation → push the response over the same WebSocket. Conversation history is persisted to MySQL; each conversation keeps at most the latest N messages (CONVERSATION_MAX_MESSAGES, default 20) and has an expiration (CONVERSATION_TTL_DAYS, default 7 days). Generation can be stopped: a stop token with a TTL is stored in Redis, and the frontend includes it when sending a stop command. On the WebSocket side, connections are capped per user (default 10) and per instance (default 1000), with an idle timeout (default 3600 seconds) and periodic heartbeat cleanup (inactive connections cleared every 300 seconds by default) so connections are not held indefinitely.
Chat flow:
Receive user message → Hybrid search for context → Assemble prompt → Call OpenAI streaming generation → Push response over the same WebSocket Conversation management:
Conversation history persisted to MySQL Each conversation keeps at most the latest N messages (CONVERSATION_MAX_MESSAGES, default 20) Conversations expire (CONVERSATION_TTL_DAYS, default 7 days) Stop generation supported via a Redis-stored stop token with TTL Connection management:
Max connections per user: 10 Max connections per instance: 1000 Idle timeout: 3600 seconds Periodic heartbeat cleanup: inactive connections cleared every 300 seconds Administration# A dedicated admin router (admin_router), separated from regular user permissions, handles user management, system configuration and more, and can be extended with auditing, operation logs and other features as needed.
Technical Challenges and Solutions# Asynchronous Document Processing# Challenge: Running parsing and embedding synchronously inside the upload API makes large files prone to timeouts and blocks the endpoint, affecting other requests.
Solution: The upload API only writes to MinIO, persists metadata and publishes a Kafka message. The consumer parses with Tika, chunks the text (chunk size 500, overlap 50), calls Embedding and writes to Elasticsearch. Parse failures are logged and degraded gracefully (if Tika fails, UTF-8 decoding is attempted; if that also fails, only metadata is stored and the message is not consumed again), preventing endless retries of the same message from blocking the queue. The upload API returns quickly while processing completes in the background.
Hybrid Search# Challenge: Vector search alone is insensitive to exact matches such as proper nouns and IDs; full-text search alone lacks semantic generalization. Neither balances “semantic similarity” and “keyword matches” on its own.
Solution: For the same set of document chunks, Elasticsearch stores both a vector field (1536 dimensions, cosine similarity) and an IK-tokenized text field. At query time both searches run in parallel, scores are normalized and fused with configurable weights (SEARCH_VECTOR_WEIGHT / SEARCH_TEXT_WEIGHT), which makes later tuning easy. In practice, both proper-noun and semantic questions get more relevant results, and RAG answers are more consistent with the knowledge base.
For the same set of document chunks, Elasticsearch stores both:
Vector field: 1536 dimensions, cosine similarity Text field: IK tokenization (ik_max_word / ik_smart) At query time both searches run in parallel, and scores are normalized and fused with configurable weights (SEARCH_VECTOR_WEIGHT / SEARCH_TEXT_WEIGHT).
Summary# The full RAG pipeline is in place, from document ingestion, parsing and embedding to hybrid search and streaming chat. Upload and parsing are decoupled asynchronously, and multi-tenant isolation via permissions and organization tags is implemented as required. Future directions include multi-model support (other Embedding and Chat models), finer-grained permissions and auditing, and iterative improvements to retrieval ranking and re-ranking.

Manshu Finetune: Chinese Medical QA LLM Fine-Tuning with Unsloth# #LLM; #Finetune; #Unsloth; #LoRA; #Qwen
LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Unsloth on a Chinese medical Q&A dataset to strengthen domain-specific question answering.
Repository: (not yet public; local project manshu_finetune)
The flowchart below summarizes the main pipeline: data preparation → fine-tuning → inference validation.
graph TD A[Chinese-medical-dialogue-data] --> B[Data Cleaning & Format Conversion] B --> C[Alpaca-format JSON] C --> D[Dataset.from_json] D --> E[Tokenize & Format] E --> F[Unsloth FastLanguageModel] F --> G[LoRA Adapter Injection] G --> H[SFTTrainer Fine-Tuning] H --> I[Save LoRA Adapter] I --> J[Merge into Full Model] J --> K[Inference Validation] K --> L[GGUF Export] Project Overview# Manshu Finetune (v0.1.0) is one of my flagship projects. It focuses on two things: LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with the Unsloth efficient fine-tuning framework, and using a real-world medical Q&A dataset (Chinese-medical-dialogue-data, about 790K Q&A pairs) to improve professional question answering in the medical domain. The project covers the full pipeline of data cleaning → format conversion → efficient fine-tuning → model merging → inference validation → GGUF export, demonstrating a solid understanding of LLM fine-tuning engineering.
Tech stack: Unsloth as the efficient fine-tuning framework (2-5x faster training, 50%-80% less GPU memory); Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the base model (Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen family, Chinese and English); LoRA/QLoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (only about 0.06% of parameters trained); Hugging Face Transformers + TRL for SFTTrainer and data processing; bitsandbytes for 4-bit quantized loading; training data from Chinese-medical-dialogue-data (covering six departments: internal medicine, surgery, pediatrics, obstetrics & gynecology, andrology, and oncology); export to GGUF for local inference with llama.cpp / Ollama.
Highlights# Efficient fine-tuning: Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel trains 2-5x faster than vanilla Transformers and cuts GPU memory by 50%-80%, so LoRA fine-tuning of a 7B model fits on a single RTX 4090 (24GB). Real medical data: The Chinese-medical-dialogue-data dataset contains about 790K real medical Q&A pairs across six departments: internal medicine (220K), surgery (116K), pediatrics (102K), obstetrics & gynecology (184K), andrology (95K), and oncology (76K). Parameter efficiency: LoRA (r=16, alpha=16) trains only about 42M parameters (0.06% of the total), injecting medical domain knowledge while preserving the base model’s general capabilities. End-to-end engineering: Covers data cleaning, format conversion, tokenization, fine-tuning, model merging, inference validation, and GGUF export, making it easy to reproduce and transfer to other domains. Multi-format export: Saves to Hugging Face format (for further training or deployment) and GGUF format (for local inference with llama.cpp / Ollama). My Role and Deliverables# I was responsible for full-stack development of data processing, fine-tuning, and inference validation, with emphasis on:
Data cleaning and format conversion: Cleaned the raw CSV data (four columns: department, title, question, answer) and converted it to Alpaca format (instruction, input, output), handling null values, malformed characters, and overly long text. Fine-tuning: Loaded a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Unsloth FastLanguageModel, injected a LoRA adapter (rank=16, alpha=16, target_modules including q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj), and ran supervised fine-tuning with SFTTrainer. Inference and export: Wrote inference scripts to validate fine-tuning results, and added support for merging LoRA into a full model and exporting GGUF (q4_k_m / q8_0) for local deployment. Category Choice Purpose Base model Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Chinese/English instruction-tuned base Fine-tuning framework Unsloth Efficient fine-tuning (2-5x speedup, 50%-80% memory savings) Fine-tuning method LoRA / QLoRA Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (only 0.06% of parameters trained) Quantization bitsandbytes 4-bit Memory optimization; trains a 7B model on a single 24GB GPU Training tool TRL SFTTrainer Supervised fine-tuning trainer Dataset Chinese-medical-dialogue-data 790K Chinese medical Q&A pairs Export format GGUF Local inference with llama.cpp / Ollama Background# General-purpose LLMs often fall short in the medical domain: limited understanding of medical terminology, and answers that may be inaccurate or not specific enough. Asking ChatGPT or a general Qwen model medical questions can yield overly generic or unprofessional advice. By fine-tuning on large-scale real medical Q&A data, this project teaches the model the phrasing, terminology, and reasoning patterns of medical answers, so it gives more professional and targeted responses in medical consultation scenarios.
Why Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct? The Qwen family performs strongly on Chinese tasks, and a 7B model can be fine-tuned on a single 24GB GPU with 4-bit quantization + LoRA, balancing quality and resource cost. The Instruct version is already instruction-tuned with good instruction-following ability, making it a good starting point for specializing in medical Q&A.
I chose Unsloth for its seamless compatibility with the Hugging Face ecosystem and its significant efficiency gains: 2-5x faster training and 50%-80% less GPU memory under the same configuration. This lets a single GPU handle training that would otherwise require multiple GPUs, lowering the barrier to experimentation and iteration.
Architecture and Technology Choices# The system uses a single-machine training setup; the entire pipeline runs on a single RTX 4090 (24GB).
Data flow: Raw data (six department CSV files from Chinese-medical-dialogue-data) is read by the cleaning script → the department, title, question, and answer columns are extracted → converted to Alpaca format as instruction (“You are now a {department} doctor. Please give advice based on the patient’s question:”), input (title + question concatenated), and output (answer) → saved as JSONL for training.
Training flow: Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained loads a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct → get_peft_model injects the LoRA adapter (r=16, lora_alpha=16, target_modules covering the attention and FFN projection layers) → SFTTrainer (from TRL) runs supervised fine-tuning with an Alpaca prompt template (learning_rate=2e-4, batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation=4, max_seq_length=2048, num_train_epochs=1) → the LoRA adapter and tokenizer are saved after training.
Inference/export flow: Load the base model and LoRA adapter → optionally call merge_and_unload to merge into a full model → run inference with Hugging Face generate or Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel.for_inference → optionally export to GGUF (q4_k_m / q8_0) for llama.cpp / Ollama.
Design rationale: Unsloth uses Triton kernel optimizations and memory management to greatly improve training efficiency without changing the model architecture, and it is fully compatible with Hugging Face Transformers, simplifying later deployment and migration. LoRA trains only low-rank incremental matrices, injecting domain knowledge while preserving the base model’s capabilities; adapters can be saved and loaded independently, making it easy to switch between tasks or domains. 4-bit quantization (NF4 + double quantization) reduces memory requirements to about 1/4 of native float16, making a 7B model trainable within 24GB of GPU memory.
Relationship to Manshu LLM: Manshu LLM focuses on implementing each Transformer module from scratch to understand the underlying principles; Manshu Finetune focuses on using existing pretrained models and efficient fine-tuning tools to quickly iterate toward a usable domain model on real data. The two are complementary, covering “deep understanding” and “practical engineering” respectively.
Key Technology Choices# Unsloth
A Triton-based efficient training framework that achieves 2-5x faster training and 50%-80% memory savings through kernel fusion and memory optimization. Fully compatible with Hugging Face Transformers: no model code changes are needed, only a different loading call. Supports mainstream architectures such as Llama, Mistral, and Qwen.
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
Injects low-rank incremental matrices (A @ B) alongside the pretrained weights and trains only the two small matrices A and B (a few hundred KB per layer at rank=16). At inference time they can be merged back into the original weights with no extra latency, or kept separate for easy task switching. Compared with full fine-tuning, it trains roughly 1000x fewer parameters, greatly reducing memory and time costs.
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
A 7B instruction-tuned model from Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen family with strong performance on Chinese tasks. The Instruct version already supports instruction following and multi-turn dialogue, making it a suitable base for medical Q&A. At 4-bit quantization the 7B weights need about 4-5GB; adding LoRA gradients and optimizer states brings total usage to about 15-18GB, which fits on a single 24GB GPU.
4-bit quantization (NF4 + double quantization)
bitsandbytes’ NF4 (Normal Float 4-bit) quantization compresses weights to 4 bits, and double quantization (quantizing the quantization constants) further reduces memory. Quantization only affects weight storage; gradients and optimizer states remain in float16/float32, so the impact on training accuracy is limited.
Alpaca format
The standard format for instruction tuning, with three fields: instruction, input (input/context), and output (expected output). A prompt template concatenates them into a complete training sample, and the model learns to generate the output from instruction + input. The format is simple and general, making it easy to adapt to different data sources.
Functional Modules# Data Cleaning and Format Conversion# The raw data comes from Chinese-medical-dialogue-data and consists of CSV files for six departments:
Department File Q&A Pairs Internal Medicine IM 220,606 Surgery Surgical 115,991 Pediatrics Pediatric 101,602 Obstetrics & Gynecology OAGD 183,751 Andrology Andriatria 94,596 Oncology Oncology 75,553 Total — 792,099 Cleaning steps:
Read each department’s CSV and normalize the encoding to UTF-8 Filter nulls: drop rows where question or answer is empty Text cleaning: strip leading/trailing whitespace and replace malformed characters (e.g., mojibake, unusual Unicode) Length filtering: drop samples where question + answer exceeds 1500 characters (to avoid overly long sequences hurting training) Deduplication: deduplicate by question, keeping the first entry (the same question may have several similar answers) Format conversion:
{ "instruction": "You are now an internal medicine doctor. Please give advice based on the patient's question:", "input": "Can people with high blood pressure take codonopsis? I have high blood pressure, and when my son-in-law visited these past two days he brought me some codonopsis to steep in water. Hello, can people with high blood pressure take codonopsis?", "output": "Patients with high blood pressure can take codonopsis orally. Codonopsis helps lower blood lipids and blood pressure and can clear waste from the blood, which offers some stabilizing and preventive benefit for patients with coronary heart disease and cardiovascular disease, so taking codonopsis regularly can help keep the risks of high blood pressure, high blood lipids and high blood sugar at bay. In addition, codonopsis replenishes qi and nourishes the blood, has a calming effect on the central nervous system, regulates digestive function, and strengthens the spleen and lungs. Thank you for your question; I hope my explanation helps." } After cleaning, the data is split 9:1 into training and validation sets and saved as JSONL.
Model Loading and LoRA Injection# Load the 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Unsloth:
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained( model_name="unsloth/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-bnb-4bit", max_seq_length=2048, dtype=None, # auto-detect load_in_4bit=True, ) Inject the LoRA adapter:
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model( model, r=16, target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=3407, ) Configuration notes:
r=16: LoRA rank, controlling the expressiveness and parameter count of the incremental matrices lora_alpha=16: Scaling factor, typically set equal to r target_modules: Modules that receive LoRA, covering attention (Q/K/V/O) and FFN (gate/up/down) use_gradient_checkpointing=“unsloth”: Unsloth-optimized gradient checkpointing for further memory savings Training Configuration and Execution# Supervised fine-tuning with TRL’s SFTTrainer:
from trl import SFTTrainer from transformers import TrainingArguments trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer, train_dataset=train_dataset, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, dataset_text_field="text", max_seq_length=2048, args=TrainingArguments( per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, warmup_steps=100, num_train_epochs=1, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=not torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), bf16=torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), logging_steps=10, eval_steps=500, save_steps=500, output_dir="outputs", optim="adamw_8bit", ), ) trainer.train() Training hyperparameters:
Parameter Value Notes per_device_train_batch_size 2 Per-GPU batch size gradient_accumulation_steps 4 Gradient accumulation; effective batch size = 8 learning_rate 2e-4 Learning rate warmup_steps 100 Warmup steps num_train_epochs 1 Training epochs (790K samples; one epoch is about 100K steps) max_seq_length 2048 Maximum sequence length optim adamw_8bit 8-bit AdamW to save optimizer-state memory Inference Validation# After training, load the LoRA adapter for inference:
FastLanguageModel.for_inference(model) inputs = tokenizer( [alpaca_prompt.format( "You are now an internal medicine doctor. Please give advice based on the patient's question:", "I've been feeling dizzy often lately and my blood pressure is a bit high. What should I pay attention to?", "" )], return_tensors="pt" ).to("cuda") outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256, temperature=0.7) print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True)) Evaluation metrics:
Human evaluation: sample 100 validation examples and compare the professionalism and relevance of answers before and after fine-tuning BLEU-4 / ROUGE-L: text similarity to reference answers (for reference only, since medical Q&A has no single correct answer) Model Export# Save the LoRA adapter:
model.save_pretrained("lora_model") tokenizer.save_pretrained("lora_model") Merge into a full model:
model.save_pretrained_merged("merged_model", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit") Export to GGUF (for llama.cpp / Ollama):
model.save_pretrained_gguf("gguf_model", tokenizer, quantization_method="q4_k_m") Supported quantization methods: q4_k_m (4-bit, recommended), q8_0 (8-bit, higher precision), f16 (half precision, lossless).
Technical Challenges and Solutions# GPU Memory Optimization# Challenge: Full fine-tuning of a 7B model requires 60-80GB of GPU memory, far beyond a single 24GB card; even with LoRA, loading and training with vanilla Transformers still needs about 30GB.
Solution:
4-bit quantized loading: bitsandbytes NF4 quantization compresses model weights from float16 (14GB) to 4-bit (about 4GB) Unsloth optimizations: Triton kernel fusion reduces intermediate activation memory, and optimized gradient checkpointing further lowers peak memory 8-bit AdamW: Optimizer states are stored in 8-bit, saving 75% of memory compared with float32 Gradient accumulation: Small batches plus gradient accumulation achieve a large effective batch while lowering per-step peak memory Training ran stably on an RTX 4090 (24GB) with peak memory of about 18GB.
Data Quality and Format# Challenge: The raw medical Q&A data is noisy (empty answers, duplicate questions, overly long text, encoding issues), which would degrade model quality if used directly.
Solution:
Multi-stage cleaning: null filtering → encoding repair → length filtering → deduplication Per-department statistics: record sample counts before and after cleaning for each department to keep the data distribution reasonable Standardized Alpaca format: a unified prompt template ensures the instruction clearly specifies the doctor role and task About 750K high-quality samples remain after cleaning, covering all six departments.
Training Stability# Challenge: Large-scale data and long-sequence training are prone to exploding gradients or non-converging loss.
Solution:
Warmup: The learning rate rises linearly from 0 to 2e-4 over the first 100 steps to avoid early gradient instability Gradient clipping: max_grad_norm=1.0 to prevent exploding gradients bf16 mixed precision: Use bf16 on supported GPUs for a wider numeric range and better stability Periodic evaluation: Evaluate on the validation set every 500 steps to monitor overfitting Training loss decreased steadily, and validation loss stabilized in the 0.8-1.0 range.
Summary# As a flagship personal project, Manshu Finetune highlights two things: first, an efficient fine-tuning approach based on Unsloth + LoRA that completes domain fine-tuning of a 7B model on a single 24GB GPU; second, the use of a real medical Q&A dataset (790K pairs) to strengthen medical question answering. The project covers the complete pipeline from data cleaning, format conversion, model loading, LoRA injection, and training to inference and GGUF export, and is reproducible and transferable to other domains.
Future directions: add fine-tuning on multi-turn dialogue data (currently single-turn Q&A); introduce DPO / RLHF to further align with human preferences; extend to other medical data sources (e.g., medical literature, clinical note summaries); deploy as an API service or integrate with a RAG system for knowledge-augmented medical Q&A.

DeepSeek-OCR 2# A document understanding model released by DeepSeek in 2026. Its core innovation is DeepEncoder V2, which uses cascaded causal reasoning to achieve 1D understanding of 2D images.
Core Innovation# Visual Causal Flow# Traditional vision encoders scan an image in a fixed order (top-left to bottom-right), while human reading follows semantically driven causal logic. DeepSeek-OCR 2 simulates this causal flow with DeepEncoder V2:
Visual tokens: bidirectional attention (preserves a global receptive field) Causal flow queries: causal attention (learnable reordering tokens) graph LR A[Image] --> B[Vision Tokenizer] B --> C[Visual Tokens] C --> D[DeepEncoder V2] D --> E[Causal Flow Queries] E --> F[DeepSeek-MoE Decoder] F --> G[Output] Architecture# Component Description Vision Tokenizer SAM-base + conv layers (80M params), 16x token compression DeepEncoder V2 Based on Qwen2-0.5B, replacing the original CLIP Decoder DeepSeek-MoE 3B (500M active) Output token count 256-1120 (on par with Gemini-1.5 Pro) Technical Details# Attention Mask# ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐ │ Bidirectional attn │ Causal attn │ │ (visual tokens) │ (causal queries) │ │ all-ones matrix │ lower-triangular │ └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘ Among visual tokens: fully visible in both directions (ViT-like) Causal flow queries: can only see preceding tokens (LLM-decoder-like) Each query can attend to all visual tokens plus preceding queries Cascaded Causal Reasoning# Encoder: semantically reorders visual tokens via causal flow queries Decoder: performs autoregressive reasoning over the reordered sequence This design bridges the gap between “2D spatial structure” and “1D causal language modeling”.
Performance# Significant improvement over DeepSeek-OCR on OmniDocBench v1.5 Much stronger visual reading-order logic Retains high-ratio token compression efficiency Related Links# GitHub DeepSeek-OCR (previous generation)

MCP (Model Context Protocol)# MCP is an open protocol released by Anthropic in 2024 for connecting LLMs to external tools and data sources. It standardizes how “AI calls tools.”
1. What It Is# MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard protocol that defines how LLM applications communicate with external services, much like a “USB protocol” for AI.
Core concepts:
Concept Description Host The LLM application that initiates requests (e.g. Claude Desktop, Cursor) Client The MCP client inside the Host; manages connections to Servers Server The service that provides tools/resources (e.g. file system, database, API) Three capabilities:
Capability Description Examples Tools Functions the LLM can call Run SQL, send email, call an API Resources Data the LLM can read File contents, database records Prompts Predefined prompt templates Code review template, summary template Architecture:
graph LR A[LLM Host] --> B[MCP Client] B <-->|JSON-RPC| C[MCP Server 1: File System] B <-->|JSON-RPC| D[MCP Server 2: Database] B <-->|JSON-RPC| E[MCP Server 3: Web API] Why MCP:
Unified standard: different tools share one protocol, so no per-LLM adapters are needed Security isolation: Servers run in separate processes with controllable permissions Ecosystem reuse: implement once, use everywhere (Claude, Cursor, custom apps) 2. Using Existing MCP Servers# Configuring in Claude Desktop# Edit the config file (macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json, Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json):
{ "mcpServers": { "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/path/to/allowed/dir"] }, "sqlite": { "command": "uvx", "args": ["mcp-server-sqlite", "--db-path", "/path/to/database.db"] } } } Configuring in Cursor# Edit .cursor/mcp.json (project-level) or the global config:

mcp-server-fetch: HTTP requests mcp-server-memory: persistent memory mcp-server-notion: Notion integration mcp-server-brave-search: Brave Search 3. Building Your Own MCP Server# Python Implementation (Recommended)# Install the SDK:
pip install mcp Minimal example (a weather lookup tool):
from mcp.server import Server from mcp.server.stdio import stdio_server from mcp.types import Tool, TextContent # Create the server server = Server("weather-server") # Define the tool list @server.list_tools() async def list_tools(): return [ Tool( name="get_weather", description="Get the weather for a given city", inputSchema={ "type": "object", "properties": { "city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name"} }, "required": ["city"] } ) ] # Implement the tool logic @server.call_tool() async def call_tool(name: str, arguments: dict): if name == "get_weather": city = arguments["city"] # A real implementation would call a weather API; this returns mock data return [TextContent(type="text", text=f"{city}: Sunny, 25°C")] raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool: {name}") # Start the server async def main(): async with stdio_server() as (read, write): await server.run(read, write, server.create_initialization_options()) if __name__ == "__main__": import asyncio asyncio.run(main()) TypeScript Implementation# Install the SDK:
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk Example:
import { Server } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js"; import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js"; const server = new Server( { name: "weather-server", version: "1.0.0" }, { capabilities: { tools: {} } } ); // List tools server.setRequestHandler("tools/list", async () => ({ tools: [{ name: "get_weather", description: "Get the weather for a given city", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { city: { type: "string" } }, required: ["city"] } }] })); // Call a tool server.setRequestHandler("tools/call", async (request) => { const { name, arguments: args } = request.params; if (name === "get_weather") { return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `${args.city}: Sunny, 25°C` }] }; } throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${name}`); }); // Start const transport = new StdioServerTransport(); server.connect(transport); Registering with a Client# Add your server to the config:
{ "mcpServers": { "my-weather": { "command": "python", "args": ["/path/to/weather_server.py"] } } } Implementing Resources (Optional)# from mcp.types import Resource @server.list_resources() async def list_resources(): return [ Resource( uri="file:///config/settings.json", name="Config file", mimeType="application/json" ) ] @server.read_resource() async def read_resource(uri: str): if uri == "file:///config/settings.json": return '{"theme": "dark", "language": "zh"}' raise ValueError(f"Unknown resource: {uri}") Debugging Tips# # Debug with MCP Inspector npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python weather_server.py # View Claude Desktop logs tail -f ~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp*.log Further Reading# Transports: stdio (local process), HTTP+SSE (remote service) Security considerations: Servers should restrict file access paths, validate input, and keep logs Official docs: modelcontextprotocol.io

Transformer# The Transformer is an architecture proposed by Google in 2017 in “Attention Is All You Need”. It is built entirely on self-attention, dropping RNNs and CNNs, and has become the foundation of modern NLP and large models.
1. What It Is# The Transformer is a sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) model architecture. Its core is self-attention, which processes the relationships between all positions in a sequence in parallel.
Key characteristics:
Parallel computation: unlike RNNs, which process tokens step by step, it handles the whole sequence at once Long-range dependencies: attention is computed directly between any two positions, with no information decay Scalability: stacking more layers and adding parameters improves capability (GPT, BERT, etc.) Overall architecture:
graph LR subgraph Encoder A[Input Embedding] --> B["#43; Positional Encoding"] B --> C[Multi-Head Attention] C --> D[Add & Norm] D --> E[Feed Forward] E --> F[Add & Norm] end subgraph Decoder G[Output Embedding] --> H["#43; Positional Encoding"] H --> I[Masked Multi-Head Attention] I --> J[Add & Norm] J --> K[Cross Attention] K --> L[Add & Norm] L --> M[Feed Forward] M --> N[Add & Norm] end F --> K N --> O[Linear + Softmax] Core components:
Component Role Self-Attention Computes association weights between each position and every other position in the sequence Multi-Head Runs several attention heads in parallel to capture features in different subspaces Positional Encoding Injects position information (sinusoidal or learned) Feed Forward Two fully connected layers + activation, applied position-wise Add & Norm Residual connection + LayerNorm, stabilizes training Three variants:
Type Representative models Structure Typical tasks Encoder-only BERT Encoder only Classification, NER, sentence similarity Decoder-only GPT, LLaMA Decoder only Text generation, dialogue Encoder-Decoder T5, BART Full structure Translation, summarization 2. How to Use It# Using Hugging Face Transformers# from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, AutoModelForCausalLM # ========== Encoder model (e.g. BERT) ========== tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-chinese") model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-chinese") text = "The Transformer is the foundation of modern NLP" inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt") outputs = model(**inputs) # Token embeddings (batch_size, seq_len, hidden_size) last_hidden = outputs.last_hidden_state # Sentence embedding (the [CLS] position) sentence_embedding = last_hidden[:, 0, :] # ========== Decoder model (e.g. GPT) ========== tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2") model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2") inputs = tokenizer("Once upon a time", return_tensors="pt") outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=50) print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0])) Common Task Examples# from transformers import pipeline # Text classification classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis") classifier("I love this movie!") # [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.99}] # Text generation generator = pipeline("text-generation", model="gpt2") generator("The future of AI is", max_length=50) # Question answering qa = pipeline("question-answering") qa(question="What is Transformer?", context="Transformer is a neural network architecture.") # Translation translator = pipeline("translation_en_to_zh", model="Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-zh") translator("Hello, world!") # Fill in the blank fill = pipeline("fill-mask", model="bert-base-chinese") fill("The weather is really [MASK] today") Common Pretrained Models# Model Type Parameters Highlights BERT Encoder 110M/340M Bidirectional encoding, suited to understanding tasks GPT-2 Decoder 117M-1.5B Autoregressive generation T5 Enc-Dec 60M-11B Unified text-to-text format LLaMA Decoder 7B-70B Open source and efficient, today’s mainstream base model Qwen Decoder 0.5B-72B Strong in both Chinese and English ChatGLM Decoder 6B-130B Optimized for Chinese dialogue Further Reading# Attention formula: $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$ Positional encoding: the original uses sinusoidal encoding; modern models mostly use RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) Optimized variants: FlashAttention (memory optimization), GQA (Grouped-Query Attention), sliding window

Word2Vec# Word2Vec is a word-vector training method introduced by Google in 2013. It maps words to dense, low-dimensional vectors so that semantically similar words end up close together in vector space.
1. What It Is# Word2Vec is a word embedding method. Its core idea is that “a word’s meaning is determined by the words around it” (the distributional hypothesis).
Key characteristics:
Dense vectors: each word is represented by a 100-300 dimensional float vector instead of a high-dimensional sparse one-hot vector Semantic similarity: semantically similar words have high cosine similarity (e.g. “king” and “queen”) Vector arithmetic: supports semantic analogies, such as king - man + woman ≈ queen Two architectures:
Architecture Input Output Characteristics CBOW Context words Center word Fast to train, suited to large corpora Skip-gram Center word Context words Better quality, suited to small corpora graph LR subgraph CBOW A1[the] --> B1[?] A2[cat] --> B1 A3[on] --> B1 A4[mat] --> B1 B1 --> C1[sat] end subgraph Skip-gram D1[sat] --> E1[the] D1 --> E2[cat] D1 --> E3[on] D1 --> E4[mat] end 2. How to Use It# Using a Pretrained Model# from gensim.models import KeyedVectors # Load pretrained word vectors (e.g. Google News, 300 dimensions) model = KeyedVectors.load_word2vec_format('GoogleNews-vectors-negative300.bin', binary=True) # Get a word vector vector = model['king'] # 300-dimensional vector # Compute similarity similarity = model.similarity('king', 'queen') # 0.65 # Find the most similar words similar_words = model.most_similar('python', topn=5) # Semantic analogy: king - man + woman = ? result = model.most_similar(positive=['king', 'woman'], negative=['man'], topn=1) # [('queen', 0.71)] Common Pretrained Models# Model Dimensions Vocabulary Source Google News 300 3M News corpus GloVe 50-300 400K Wikipedia + Gigaword fastText 300 2M Common Crawl Tencent Chinese 200 8M Chinese corpus 3. How to Train It# Training with Gensim# from gensim.models import Word2Vec # Prepare the corpus: a list of tokenized sentences sentences = [ ['i', 'love', 'machine', 'learning'], ['deep', 'learning', 'is', 'fun'], ['natural', 'language', 'processing', 'is', 'NLP'], # ... more sentences ] # Train the model model = Word2Vec( sentences, vector_size=100, # vector dimensions window=5, # context window size min_count=1, # minimum word frequency sg=1, # 0=CBOW, 1=Skip-gram workers=4, # number of parallel threads epochs=10, # number of training epochs ) # Save and load model.save('word2vec.model') model = Word2Vec.load('word2vec.model') # Use vector = model.wv['machine'] similar = model.wv.most_similar('learning') Key Parameters# Parameter Description Recommended vector_size Vector dimensions 100-300 window Context window 5-10 min_count Minimum word frequency filter 5-10 sg 0=CBOW, 1=Skip-gram 1 for small corpora negative Number of negative samples 5-20 epochs Number of training epochs 5-20 Training Tips# Corpus size: at least millions of sentences; the larger the corpus, the better the results Tokenization quality: Chinese text must first be segmented with a tool like jieba Window size: small windows capture syntactic relations, large windows capture semantic relations Negative sampling: faster and more widely used than Hierarchical Softmax Further Reading# GloVe: combines global word co-occurrence statistics with local context fastText: supports subwords, so it can handle out-of-vocabulary words ELMo / BERT: contextual, dynamic word vectors that resolve polysemy
